Q: How should ACKs be handled for a 10 byte packet traveling across communication hops, starting from a JS client (BLE → UART → MCU → UART → BLE) A:

You have two different problems you are trying to solve with your "ACK":

  1. Transport-layer flow control (resolving Bluetooth packet losses, ethernet frame collisions, etc)
  2. Command feedback

You need to implement two separate mechanisms, instead of relying on your command feedback to retry lost packets.

Acknowledge and (as necessary) retransmit every message (whether or not it is a command) on a per-hop basis. And send the command response as a separate message (which will also be acknowledged per-hop during transport) from the end MCU back to the UI.

The per-hop acknowledgement is low latency, related to the transmission time on that hop, not the round trip time, and can use exponential backoff on hops where that is appropriate. Lost packets don't produce duplicate transmissions up and down the whole chain.

The command response is now abstracted from the link-level retransmits, so it doesn't need exponential backoff.

Q: pandas last 3 weeks same day average in groups A:

Implementation turned out rather tedious but this code should do the expected.

Idea is to:

  1. Split dataframe into two rather than using groupby
  2. Reindex both on date filling the date gaps
  3. Calculate rolling averge in both
  4. Merge results back into one dataframe

Gaps are filled with NaNs so they are not taken into account in mean evaluation. That makes rolling average be always truly calculated using available data from last 3 weeks.

def fill_missing_dates(df):
    idx = pd.date_range(df["Date"].min(), df["Date"].max(), freq="D")
    df.index = df["Date"]
    df = df.reindex(idx)
    return df


# Format date column
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"])


# Split dataframes based on group
df_1 = df[df["Group"].str.contains("Group 1")]
df_2 = df[df["Group"].str.contains("Group 2")]

# fill empty slots with np.nan by reindexing on date range
df_1 = fill_missing_dates(df_1)
df_2 = fill_missing_dates(df_2)

# Rolling mean with 3 week time range
df_1[["Data 1 L3W Av", "Data 2 L3W Av"]] = (
    df_1[["Data 1", "Data 2"]].rolling("21D").mean()
)
df_2[["Data 1 L3W Av", "Data 2 L3W Av"]] = (
    df_2[["Data 1", "Data 2"]].rolling("21D").mean()
)

# Set indexes for multi key join
df_1 = df_1.set_index(["Date", "Group"])
df_2 = df_2.set_index(["Date", "Group"])

# Merge results
df_result = df_1.combine_first(df_2)

# Join main df with results
df = df.join(df_result[["Data 1 L3W Av", "Data 2 L3W Av"]], on=[
             "Date", "Group"])

Q: Python Error: InsertError: replace() argument 2 must be str, not None A:

You can try:

html = htmlfile.read().replace("%TRACKINGNO%", TrackingNo or "")

If TrackingNo is None, it'll default to "". (you can use any string value you like there).

If TrackingNo exists, it'll use the value of TrackingNo.

Q: How can I flock LOCK_EX if there is always a LOCK_SH? A:

You don't need to use any locking.

Use rename().

Assuming this is a POSIX system and you're running on a local filesystem that supports atomic rename() operations (and if you're trying to do file locking on any non-local, network file system, give up now), and every file access by a reader is done via open()/read()/close() operations, don't bother using locks.

Simply write a new file in the same filesystem as the working copy, then call rename( "/path/to/new/file", /path/to/working/copy" ). Any open file descriptor on the original working copy of the file will remain valid, allowing any reader to have an unmodified copy of the data, and any open() call made after the rename() will use the new copy. And once the last open file descriptor on the old file is closed, the old file will be deleted.

And you wondered why Unix allows things like deleting or renaming a file while it's open? Now you know.
